definition: A lawful permanent resident (LPR) is a non-citizen who has been granted the right to live and work in the United States indefinitely. LPRs are issued a Permanent Resident Card, commonly known as a “green card,” which serves as proof of their status. LPRs enjoy many of the same rights as U.S. citizens, such as the ability to work without restrictions, own property, and receive certain public benefits. They are also required to file U.S. income taxes. However, LPRs cannot vote in federal elections and are ineligible for some government jobs, security clearances, and scholarships. Naturalization as a U.S. citizen generally requires prior LPR status and at least five years of continuous residence (three years for certain applicants, such as spouses of U.S. citizens). The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) establishes several broad categories under which an individual may obtain LPR status. These include family-based immigration, employment-based immigration, the Diversity Visa Lottery, refugee or asylum status, and certain other humanitarian provisions. The number of LPR visas issued each year is subject to statutory limits. LPR status, though permanent, can be lost or revoked. It may be considered abandoned if an LPR leaves the United States for extended periods without proper authorization, such as a reentry permit. It may also be revoked if the individual commits certain crimes, engages in immigration fraud, or is otherwise found removable under the INA.
